sentences.text: Trace the air pathway.
Air enters through the nose or mouth.
The nasal cavity filters, warms, and humidifies air.
The pharynx has named regions: the nasopharynx behind the nasal cavity, the oropharynx behind the oral cavity, and the laryngopharynx farther down.
These regions are not simply alternate names for the nose and mouth.
The airway shares part of its route with the digestive pathway before the routes separate.

sentences.text: The larynx contains the vocal folds and connects the pharynx to the trachea.
During swallowing, coordinated movements protect the airway; the epiglottis helps cover the laryngeal opening.
The trachea then carries air toward the lungs.
Definitions of the upper-lower airway boundary differ among courses, so this lesson will name the actual structures rather than make the boundary itself a physiological rule.

sentences.text: The trachea divides into the right and left main bronchi.
Inside the lungs, branches become smaller bronchi and bronchioles.
The right lung normally has three lobes, and the left has two.
The conducting airways transport air.
Farther along, the respiratory zone includes respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, and alveoli.
Follow the route rather than treating the pleura or diaphragm as structures that air passes through.

sentences.text: Terminal bronchioles are the final part of the conducting zone.
They do not contain the alveoli needed for ordinary gas exchange.
Respiratory bronchioles, which come after them, have alveoli in their walls and begin the respiratory zone.
Anatomical dead space is air in conducting passages that does not participate in gas exchange.
Physiological dead space also includes ventilated alveoli that receive too little blood flow for effective exchange.

sentences.text: The visceral pleura covers the lung surface.
The parietal pleura lines the inside of the thoracic wall.
A thin fluid layer between them reduces friction and helps the lungs follow movements of the chest wall.
This is normally a potential space, not a large air-filled gap.
Air or excess fluid entering the pleural space can interfere with expansion.
Keep the pleura separate from the branching airway route.

sentences.text: Watch inspiration.
The diaphragm contracts and moves downward, becoming flatter.
External intercostal muscles help lift and expand the rib cage.
Thoracic volume increases, the lungs expand, and alveolar pressure briefly falls below atmospheric pressure.
Air moves inward down that pressure gradient.
The diaphragm does not pull air directly through a tube; its movement changes the dimensions and pressure relationships of the thorax.

sentences.text: During quiet expiration, the diaphragm relaxes and the elastic recoil of the respiratory system helps reduce lung volume.
Alveolar pressure briefly rises above atmospheric pressure, and air moves out.
Quiet expiration is usually passive.
Forced breathing can recruit additional muscles, including abdominal and accessory inspiratory muscles.
One breath contains an inspiratory phase and an expiratory phase; count a complete cycle, not each movement as a separate breath.

sentences.text: At the alveolus, a very thin barrier separates air from pulmonary capillary blood.
Oxygen diffuses from alveolar air into blood because its partial pressure is higher in the alveolus.
Carbon dioxide diffuses in the opposite direction because its partial pressure is higher in the arriving blood.
Diffusion itself is passive.
A large surface area, a thin barrier, ventilation, and blood flow all support effective exchange.

sentences.text: Ventilation means moving air into and out of the lungs.
Perfusion means blood flow through tissue, including pulmonary capillaries.
External respiration is gas exchange between alveoli and blood.
Internal respiration is exchange between systemic blood and tissues.
Cellular respiration is the chemical process by which cells use energy substrates, often consuming oxygen and producing carbon dioxide.
These ideas connect, but they are not interchangeable names for the same event.

sentences.text: Carbon dioxide participates in the bicarbonate buffer system.
If other factors remain similar, retaining more carbon dioxide tends to lower blood pH, while removing more tends to raise it.
Arterial blood pH is normally tightly regulated around seven point three five to seven point four five.
The lungs and kidneys both contribute to acid-base regulation.
A visible chest rise alone does not tell us whether ventilation is removing carbon dioxide adequately.

sentences.text: Networks in the medulla and pons generate and shape the breathing pattern.
Central chemoreceptors respond mainly to changes related to carbon dioxide and cerebrospinal-fluid pH.
Peripheral chemoreceptors also respond to oxygen, carbon dioxide, and pH.
Sensory input through nerves, including the vagus, modifies the pattern.
It is too simple to say that chemoreceptors alone initiate every breath or that the vagus always increases breathing rate.

sentences.text: Follow an oxygen molecule from the alveolus into pulmonary blood, through the left atrium and left ventricle, and into the systemic circulation.
Then follow carbon dioxide in the opposite overall journey, from tissues back to the lungs.
Before continuing, explain the difference between moving air and exchanging gas.
Which muscle drives most quiet inspiration, and why do terminal bronchioles conduct air rather than exchange gases?
